utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. Second, we usual have a break at a quarter to 4.00 until quarter past 4.00, and then again at approximately 5.30 if we still need so much time. Mr. Vanderostyne, you will first be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Mahindaratne you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderostyne. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, madam, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, did you have the opportunity to examine that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, madam. I have gone through it extensively yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you find that the contents of the statement accurately reflects what you stated to the members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call on the screen document number 5163, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, are the contents of your statement true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: They are true to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if I were to ask you the questions that were asked of you by the member of the Office of the Prosecutor on 15th March and 1st July to the court, would your responses be the same as those reflected in your statement?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, they would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you look at the screen in front of you, Mr. Vanderostyne, could you identify that this is your statement, and if we could flick through to the signature page, please.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: It is my statement and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this statement in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the written submissions, I understand there's no objection against admission. Therefore, Mr. Registrar, this would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P321 is admitted into evidence. Since we're dealing at this moment with admission of evidence, I noticed, Ms. Mahindaratne, that the Prosecution has applied for adding to its 65 ter list two documents in the written submissions that was the CV of Mr. Vanderostyne, and it was a map showing the itinerary. From the written submissions from the Defence, I do understand that there is no objection against that. And I also now understand that you want to add to your 65 ter list two new documents by the numbers of 5172, and -- let me just see whether I'm not making any mistake. Yes, I think it is 5172 and 5173 which you'd like to add to your 65 ter list as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, but there has been an adjustment. I would now wish to make an application only with regard to document number 5173, 5173. I'm no longer sustaining the application with regard to document number 5172.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I took it from e-mail exchanges which were copied to the Chamber that there is no objection against adding 5173 to the 65 ter list. I see all counsel nodding. Then, Ms. Mahindaratne, the Chamber decides that the CV of this witness, which was - I'm just looking now at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That would be, Mr. President, 5164, document number 5164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is called here the resume dated the 1st of January, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber grants the request to add 5164, 5165, and 5173 to the Prosecution's 65 ter list. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, these are some procedural issues which we have to bother -- we shouldn't bother you with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just read the summary briefly before proceeding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And again, I take it you have explained to Mr. Vanderostyne what the purpose of reading it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Edmond Vanderostyne is a journalist who worked as a reporter, a senior writer, and an editorialist with a leading Belgian group of daily newspapers, De Standaard, for over three decades. He has reported on conflicts throughout the world, including in Rwanda and Afghanistan. He was present and reported on events in Sarajevo and Vukovar during the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Vanderostyne has received numerous awards for his journalistic work. Mr. Vanderostyne was present in the Krajina on assignment in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm. He travelled in Sectors North and South and observed extensive destruction of property due to shelling and arson, looting, and evidence of the hasty flight of the Serb population. He observed the presence of Croatian military forces and civilian police, including military and civilian police check-points en route to Gracac and Knin. In Gracac, he observed destruction of property, including several burning houses. He further observed members of the MUP Special Police forces looting in Gracac and interviewed a senior officer of the Special Police present in Gracac. Mr. Vanderostyne provides photographs of some of the scenes witnessed by him. He has written numerous press articles on his observations in the Krajina. That concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. If have you further questions to put to the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, now, when you made your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you provided the -- provided copies of press articles written by you as well as some photographs, a map, and your resume. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, did you examine that material?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it yesterday, and that's exactly what I had seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the contents of that material are accurately explained in your statement? You in fact explained those materials?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up document 3230, please, on the screen. Mr. President, this is part of the 92 ter submissions, so I -- do I just call up the number, the documents and the number is given or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check with Mr. Registrar. The witness statement, 5163, no attachments are -- is it just a statement, or is it with attachments?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may assist, Mr. President, there are no attachments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then they need separate numbers. Mr. Registrar, this newspaper article of the Belgian newspaper De Standaard original in Dutch would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then P322 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I ask a couple of questions before I -- on this document, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, do you know the press article on your screen?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, is this article based on what you observed on your assignment in the Krajina, in particular what you observed in Gracac on 8 August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: That's correct. It is the newspaper of the Wednesday, 9th August, reporting what I had witnessed Tuesday, late afternoon, on my way from Zagreb to Knin, and it was -- it has been filed from Sibenik at the coast, Croatian coast, where there was at last a telephone available.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up documents number 3717, which is a photograph of -- going up to 3719, three photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, do you want to tender them as three photographs, one series, one number?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: One number would be appropriate, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Will there BE any objections against the photographs to be tendered? Not. Then, Mr. Registrar, the series of three photographs, 3717 up to and including 3719 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P 323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P323 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I call up Exhibit 3720 up to and including 3723, four photographs, and here, too, Mr. President, if one number is given to the series it would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this series of photographs becomes Exhibit P324.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P324 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could I keep that photograph on the screen, please, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vanderostyne, if I could draw your attention to paragraph 31 of your statement. Now, there you refer to your observations in Gracac on 8th August, and you say that in relation to your -- you say that you saw "a Delta unit, a group of about 50 men, possibly hundreds, spread over the central square and in the streets around. They also appeared to be organised. We parked the car. I told the photographer to take pictures while we distracted the officers." Then in the same paragraph, going further down, up to line 15, you record what you observed there. You say: "I saw a vehicle with a sign bearing the name Delta VK," I refer to the picture numbered and you have given a number, "and a blue truck bearing a plate with Cyrillic letters and being loaded with goods - TV, shoes, bags, suitcases - I called it war booty treasure." Now, there is a photograph on the screen. You referred to in your statement a blue truck with a plate, bearing Cyrillic number plate. Is that the truck you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: That's it. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this picture shows a man in olive-green uniform loading what seems to be a television into the truck. Now, in your statement at paragraph 30, if I could go to the paragraph before, you say: "We drove straight through the city of Gracac and did not stop. After we left the city, we discussed what we had seen, that uniformed Croatian people were looting." Now, can you tell Court as to what was the uniform worn by those men you saw looting?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: The uniform was khaki, Olive-green, and they had a yellow ribbon on their shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you indicate whether can you see in your -- those men that you saw in that particular uniform, I'm not talking about the people that -- individuals, but the uniform. Can you see in this picture?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, it is that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is the uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: This is the uniform I had observed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we can go on to the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it the witness is now pointing at the person who is central in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Closest to the blue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- truck. Yes. Please proceed. Ms. Mahindaratne, there are three persons on this screen --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and -- although I could not immediately see whether these others are wearing uniforms, but could I not exclude for that possibility. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for that. If we could move to the next photograph, which bears the ERN 9981 on top. That would be the next photograph in the series.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you see scenes like this in Gracac on 8th August, Mr. Vanderostyne?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Oh yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you explain to Court based on your observations what this man is supposed to be doing here.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: He is a member of that Delta unit to whose commander I have been spoken, I spoke, and he's cutting short some wires for stealing that private vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next photograph, please. That's the document bearing ERN 9982, which is the next one in the series. And if we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vanderostyne, paragraph 31, you referred to seeing a vehicle with the letters Delta VK written on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could go on to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the vehicle, or were there other vehicles with the same inscription that you saw in Gracac on 8th August?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Whether there were other vehicles with that inscription, I would not be sure today. But I have seen that vehicle with that inscription painted on the -- on that vehicle, yes, indeed, in Gracac. On that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vanderostyne, can I just take you to your paragraph 33 of your statement. You refer to seeing in Gracac -- you say: "I saw men in khaki uniforms." When you use the word "khaki uniforms," are you referring to the olive-green uniforms that we're seeing in these pictures?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Going back to paragraph 31, you -- and I read it to you a little while ago, you refer to instructing your photographer to take pictures while you distracted the officers. Now, how long did you spend in Gracac on 8th August? And if you could answer briefly.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I shall answer briefly. We -- our focus was to witness the situation in Knin, yet we what we observed in Gracac and between Gospic and Gracac was a story in itself. However, we were very late that afternoon, and we were very short in time. So we drove very fast through the city of Gracac, and it was only after we had left that we stopped the car. I was there with a colleague and a photographer; we were three. We stopped the car, and we looked to each other, asking, Have you seen what I have seen? Driving at a -- fastly through the city centre, and every one of us had seen that same scene of looting and khaki uniform. So we stopped, and we decided after all although we were quite scared to drive back into Gracac. We drove very slowly, not in an aggressive mood, and -- because it was a quite intense situation. Then we drove very slowly, windows opened, nobody should be -- should feel threatened. And we parked the car, and we tried to be relaxed, so in a more or less relaxed way we went to a little group of those soldiers that were drinking, that were relaxing under a tree. And we started small talk, but I knew very well that I had maybe five, at a maximum ten minutes, and things would turn, turn more aggressive. I was sure about that. So I knew I have to ask three, four, maybe five very precise questions, and then I have to move as soon as I can. So after -- after engaging in small talk with the accordionist, I ask him very quickly, Who is your commander, who is in charge, and he showed me a man on the opposite of the street or the opposite of the square, and I did that in order that everyone should feel at ease. Nobody should feel threatened. Everybody, the military and we ourselves, we were surprised. Anyway, to make it short, that is the way how I got introduced to that lieutenant. He saw me walking from over the street, hands open, in an open, non-aggressive mood, and I -- so I could speak to that lieutenant, just fire my four or five questions. How long have I been in Gracac, in all, less than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it during that time that your photographer managed to take these photographs?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes madam. When we moved from that accordionist to the lieutenant, I told my -- the photographer, Frank Dejongh, I told him, Frank, you have less than five minutes; you go around; you do your own work; I'm speaking to that lieutenant; I'm asking the questions, and we're away within five or ten minutes, and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, in the same paragraph you refer to having that conversation with the officer who was present there. And you say that he identified the unit as the Delta unit of Vinkovci or from Eastern Slavonia or, dash, Eastern Slavonia. My interpretation was that they were a Special Police unit. He literally said, you do understand after all what special forces mean? " And then in paragraph 32, you further go on and describe your conversation with him regarding the emblems, the insignia on his uniform. Now, according to the cover page of your statement, Mr. Vanderostyne, there is no indication that you speak Croatian. Can you explain to Court as to how you communicated with the officer.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could -- Mr. Vanderostyne, if you could be brief because we have limited time.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I don't speak Urdu in Pakistan, either, or Kinyarwanda in Rwanda, either, so no, I don't speak Croatian. I know -- I knew a few words to -- to make people feel at ease, but I don't speak Croatian. We speak -- we spoke, I spoke English in the first place, and I would get an answer in broken English or in German, and it would continue in broken English or in German, but -- well, that's it. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when I in fact asked you this question in -- during the course of proofing, you referred to your notebook which you carried on 8 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could, I don't want to waste time you going through the book. Can you explain to Court as to whether you had specific notes of that conversation in that book, and I know that have you brought it to Court today.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, madam, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm on my feet. I apologise for interrupting. If I may just inquire, I don't believe that the Gotovina Defence received a proofing note for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was no additional information provided by this witness to -- including a proofing note. This was a clarification. I asked a question as to how he communicated, and he said the same thing, which I don't believe is additional information. This matter has been dealt with even in his statement, and I believe what we include in a proofing note is new information that has not been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, so therefore, there is nothing new that should be disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vanderostyne, can you tell Court where -- if it is possible for you to recall, where was the looting activity that you observed taking place in relation to where the officer was standing and where you were conversing with the officer?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: It was a central square of Gracac, and you saw soldiers -- not soldiers. Excuse me. You saw those khaki uniform, I will call them, all around. Well, I have no geographic orientation or it is hard to describe, but people were spread out over that -- over that square. Half of them were relaxing, were drinking a bottle of wine, were playing accordion, were just relaxing. At another site, you saw a bus from Vinkovci, which I thought, which is my interpretation, which I thought would bring back those people to the area of origin. The lieutenant told me their job had almost been done, and then at the opposite side of the square there were several little groups that were looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the opposite side of the square is in the same vicinity as you were when you took -- were talking to the officer?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's very -- off the road it is quite small, and I'm speaking more specifically on the side from where we have entered from Gospic. So we drove through the city centre from left to right, let's say, and on the central square, the lieutenant say -- was in the middle, and then the looting took place, rather, at the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now based on your testimony, Mr. Vanderostyne, your photographer Mr. Frank Dejongh was able to photograph looting by uniformed personnel within that short period. Now, are you in a position to say as to how those personnel reacted to the photographer attempting to record what was going on?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I have, of course, no first-hand witness of that. I was not present with the photographer. I had -- I directed him to move and to -- to go around and take his pictures. But when he came back, he told that people reacted -- in the first place they were quite friendly. They were even laughing. There was a kind of pride, and I have observed that at many other occasions also. Even if they're committing crimes, there's a kind of pride. They're proud of what they are doing. They are leaving their signature. So in the first two minutes, it's at ease and it's comfortable and even relaxed. They're proud of what they are doing, but he told me, and indeed, it's not -- that's what he told me, because I was not with him, he told me that it turned very sour very fast, and that was what -- what I would have excepted also.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up documents number -- I'm sorry Mr. President. I don't believe that we gave a P number to this series of photographs. May I tender them in evidence, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these were admitted as Exhibit P324.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was what my recollection was. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar. May I call up documents number 3724, 3725, and 3713, three photographs, all in the same series. While they're being -- the photograph is coming up --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, you referred to discussing with the officer, you had a conversation with the emblems on his uniform. Now, you also referred to seeing yellow ribbons on the olive-green uniforms. If you could just focus on the -- get a close-up on the emblem on the left sleeve of the ... Now, we note that this emblem contains the word "Policija." Is this one of the emblems that you saw in Gracac on 8 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, madam. That's the emblem the lieutenant showed me. I asked the lieutenant, What unit are you with, and he showed, he himself showed the emblem on his -- on his arm, and that's the emblem he showed me. That's -- that I have seen myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you see this emblem on any of the soldiers who you saw were -- or the personnel in uniform who were looting or who were surrounding the centre, the other personnel?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I was not focussed on that. I have not seen it, but of course, these are the pictures that had been taken that afternoon, and I recognise it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move on to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We see a group of men in olive-green uniforms. Is that you in the foreground?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, and I was younger.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could -- actually, the next picture is better for the emblem. If you could move on to the next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it is 748 -- I'm sorry, 3713. And if we could focus on that sleeve of the -- if you could get a -- this emblem is not that clear. It indicates a vertical line and three horizontal lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing this insignia?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, I have not seen it myself, but it's clearly -- I have not seen it because I was not focussed on that. I was just speaking, and I had very limited time. But it is clearly that this person is one of the group I have been observing, and, yeah, that's the insignia that's on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were these the emblems that you discussed with -- that you discussed with the unit commander?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: This precise emblem I did not discuss. He showed me the MUP insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this into evidence, please, three photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Three photographs, they appear in two categories, but it's 3724, 3725, and 3713. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P325.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P325 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up map number 5164, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, you provided a map to the Office of the Prosecutor which indicated the route you took --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 5165, beg your pardon. 5165.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You indicated the route that you took from Karlovac to Gracac and then to Knin on 8 August 1995. Do you recall that? It will take a little while to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think we need to turn it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the left. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you could just focus on that red line. For the record, Mr. President, I'll indicate the places.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You indicated the route you took on 8th August and the places you -- or the main areas that you went through. For the record, starting with Karlovac; the next circle is Sinj [sic]; then, next one is Otocac; Gospic; Gracac; Sucevici; and then Knin. Is that correct, Mr. Vanderostyne?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. It is a copy of the exact map that I have used, and those circles have been written by me on that afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- point something out to avoid later confusion in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first town is Senj not to be confused with Sinj, which is actually south of Knin, just so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. I take it, Witness, that you agree with what Mr. Misetic just said, that it's not the town of Sinj, which is south of but that it's a village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. We were heading in a general direction of Sinj, I think which is on the coast -- on the coast, so we -- I have not been in Sinj, but we were heading in that direction, and that might be why it is circled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I tender the map into evidence, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, Mr. Registrar, the map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P326 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, you also submitted your resume which includes information of your experience to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could call up document number 5164, please. While the document is coming up -- yes. And if this could be tendered into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Therefore, Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P327, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P327 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, those are the documents included in the 92 ter submissions. I have just two more documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, yesterday during proofing I showed you prints, of two emblems, and if I could call up document number 5173, please. You looked at those prints, and you said you could recognise them. Can you recollect that --

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: It's the emblem the lieutenant of the Delta unit showed me on his shoulder on the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we go on to the next page, please, of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen this emblem before?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I have seen it before, but I did not see it personally in Gracac because I have not been -- I was not focussed on that. But I have seen that emblem on the pictures of -- that the photographer have -- has taken of the people that were looting in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document into evidence, please? It contains two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there are no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P328 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could call up document number 458, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, there will be a document on the screen, and I appreciate if you not have seen that document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could on B/C/S move to page number 5; and on the English copy, to page 12 and 13. Page 5 on B/C/S and page 12 and 13 on the English copy. Mr. President, may I tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is more or less from the bar table, I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm just making use of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because the witness apparently has no knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar, that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P329 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have just a few more questions, Mr. Vanderostyne. If could I take you to paragraph 12 up to 14 in your statement. You refer to coming by one civilian police check-point and thereafter several military check-points after leaving Karlovac. And, in fact, you refer to being stopped at the military check-points and not being allowed to move onwards and having to backtrack and take what you called secondary routes. Now, my question to you is: Who manned the military check-points, soldiers or military police?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: From between Zagreb and Karlovac, there were no check-points. Leaving Karlovac to the south, we encountered police check-point. They told us that the road was not open and that we -- well, anyway, they let us proceed anyhow because we had a permit of the Ministry of Defence. That was a police check-point. Afterwards, between the south of Karlovac and the point where we turned to the left into Krajina proper, that -- that were military check-points. Those were military people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Vanderostyne, are you in a position to say whether they were mere soldiers or military police? You know the difference.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, I'm not in a position now to say whether it is military police or army personnel. They were army -- they were military people. There were no police. That I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But just to understand you fully, you said there were military people; there were no police. Do you exclude for the possibility that they were military police, which are military but at the same time police, or would you say these were non-police military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't exclude that they were military police because I have not formally identified them as such. Anyway, it were military positions. It were defensive positions kind of -- well, defensive positions. They had pits and there were trees that were -- that had barricaded them, so I think, Mr. President, it was, rather, conscripts or -- or common military unit in defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on that main route you indicated, Mr. Vanderostyne, which you indicated on the map, was there that much of traffic, and I'm referring to civilian traffic or civilians in numbers, walking through that area?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, madam. There was no traffic at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said in your statement that as a result of not being allowed to move on from the military check-points, you were required to backtrack and take secondary routes to bypass the check-point. Now, were those secondary routes or did you see much traffic in those secondary routes or many civilians walking around?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: On those secondary roads, I saw no -- no traffic. There were -- yet there were civilians around, yes. There were -- you had the villages and the hamlets, and there were people around, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I'm not talking about residents of hamlets and the villages you passed through. But were there -- did you see sort of an influx or people coming into the area through those secondary routes?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No madam, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, taking you to paragraph 29. You said -- this is regarding your entry into Gracac. You say: "Upon entering Gracac, I saw several houses that were just set on fire. There was smoke all over the outskirts. I saw small groups of young men." It goes on. And then onto the next page, you say: "I notice many plumes of smoke." It's -- there's a typo there, indicated as blooms. "I remarked in my journal that almost all houses in the 50 kilometres or so between Gospic and Gracac were destroyed." Then further on, you go on to say: "The city of Gracac was not yet on fire, but the outskirts was burning." Now, my question to you is, How big is Gracac and including the town, that entire area you talk about, the outskirts and the town of Gracac, how big was that?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Hard to say, but it's a small town -- a small -- really a small town. You drive through, and I -- it is a small town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, based on your observations, according to the topography that you observed, could you notice the plumes of smoke in the outskirts of Gracac from the town?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: From the town I have seen because I really was not focussed on that. I had seen it, anyway, entering Gracac, but once I wasn't on that central square I did not look anymore on the fires at the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, my question is not whether you looked. Based on what you know of Gracac, you know, the topography, for instance, if someone stood in the town and looked up, could they see the smoke around?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I imagine so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Taking you to paragraph 38 - and I'm on my last few questions - you refer to -- about the fourth line. You say: "There were check-points upon entering Knin, but we were not halted." Can you tell the Court as to who was manning these check-points? Was it the military or the civilian police or some other force?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I would think it was the military -- it was -- it were military check-points. Maybe I have that in my notebook, but ... No, I have no specific mention of that, but Knin was -- the garda, the army was all present, you see? Before Knin and before Gracac, I had seen -- those were all grey/blue uniforms of ordinary Croatian police. In Gracac, it had been the olive-green khaki uniforms of that Delta unit and in Knin it was the garda, the normal military units and conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall about how many check-points you had to go through before you entered Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: In all? Since Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just at the point of entry to Knin. Was there just one or -- I'm referring to paragraph 38 where you say: "There were check-points upon entering Knin." So obviously after entering Knin or maybe just at the point.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I think that might be an exaggeration. Probably there was one check-point. There might have been others, but it is it not -- I mean, I feel it is not very relevant because I could pass through anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on, taking to you paragraph 31, back again, the last sentence, Mr. Vanderostyne. You say with regard to your observations: "I witnessed looting and burning" -- No, you go and say "I made a note in my journal that they were leaving their signatures just like I had seen the Serbs do in other places. I witnessed looting and burning on a major scale." Now, can you clarify what you meant by major scale?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, sure, I can. Looting on -- burning on a major scale, those were not isolated incidents. It was between Gospic and Gracac. I don't know what is the distance, but it might -- it is tens of kilometres, maybe 50 kilometres. I don't know. Anyway, that can be checked. Between Gospic and Gracac, the whole countryside was in fire. And I remember, Mr. President, at one time we were crossing a little -- a little -- a small -- a little hill, and -- and you saw the countryside as far as could you look and everywhere, everywhere, every farm, every barn, every annex, every house in the countryside, I mean, not in the villages, but every single building in the countryside was on fire. So that is what I mean, on a major scale. About looting on a major scale, I mean, again, those were not isolated incidents. It was organised. It was -- it happened amongst others by people in uniform, also by civilians, civilians probably -- which I interpreted came from the Sibenik Croatian coast. But there were no -- there were no isolated incidents. In the outskirts of Gracac, I saw trucks fully loaded with booty, I shall call it, coming and going. I saw police vehicles being loaded with booty. Not a single one, but several cars and at several places, and I saw at the central square looting, plundering by that Delta unit at several places. Those were not isolated incidents, and they were organised. That's what I mean by "major scale."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderostyne. Just taking you quickly to paragraph 14 of your statement. Line 3, you say: "Everywhere we saw a lot of damage as a result of bombardments. People were scared, and I noted this in my diary." And when say a lot of damage due to bombardment, what are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: On this precise place, I'm referring to Karlovac, I think, to the damage I had seen in Karlovac and people that were scared. Because in Karlovac, we had left our car and spoken to people and walked around, and that observation is just after leaving Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. Vanderostyne, just the last question. If you could go to paragraph 25. There, you refer to having written an article with regard to what you observed, and you say: "It describes the exodus of the Serbs. It was a humiliating experience for them. On display were 150.000 Serbs traveling 5 to 10 kilometres per hour through enemy territory." Now, did you see this convoy of refugees that you're referring to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, madam, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when you saw the convoy of refugees?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That is after we returned from Sibenik, so in Sibenik we were on the Wednesday, the 9th, visiting the hospital and the victims. Then I returned to Zagreb, and after Zagreb I moved on for the follow-up story to Osijek in Eastern Slavonia, and that was on that day, so probably three days later along the highway or the express way, and there were both convoys and isolated -- I mean, the highway had been closed off for normal traffic, and Serbs from Krajina were moving in very slow vehicles and wagons towards Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say three days later, so that brings you around the 12th of August, 13th, 14th, that period?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Probably it was on Saturday or the Friday, but -- well, I cannot -- unless I should check in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That should be all right. That's fine, Mr. Vanderostyne. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes the examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Your estimate of 30, 40 minutes was not of an accuracy which the Chamber prefers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- we could do two things. We could -- Mr. Mikulicic, we could start now with the cross-examination. We also could take an early break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think we could use an early break, especially having in mind the request of the witness before the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then take a break now. We will resume at ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderostyne. I'm Goran Mikulicic representing General Cermak, just as His Honour the Judge said. I'm going to put a number of questions to you, so I would like to ask you to answer them according to your best recollection. Sir, can you please tell us why you were surprised when the Croatian Defence Ministry allowed you to visit the territory that was liberated in the Storm action?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sir. There were of course many, many foreign journalists in Zagreb awaiting for leaving for Knin, and for one reason or another, I and my crew and my colleague and the photographer received that permit and all my other colleagues, all my other colleagues as far as I know in the Intercon had not received a permit like that, so -- well, that I have no explanation for it, but that was my surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the following next days other journalists also were allowed to visit that area?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, sir, I was not -- I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like the registry to place the map on the screen, P326, which is the map that the witness previously marked. While we're waiting for the map to appear, you said in your statement, and I'm referring to today's date, that you left the car in Karlovac and that you talked with some people, and also, you said that people were scared because there was a lot of shelling or bombing. Did I understand what you said correctly?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In Karlovac, I spoke to people and they were scared. There had been shelling and there had been bombing, and some of them, I recall, did not really know where to find refuge or to hide for the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know which side in the conflict bombarded Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, I don't know, sir. I suppose both sides have met or have -- have exchanged fire, as it happens in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that throughout the whole wartime period Karlovac was in Croatian hands and that bit was exclusively bombarded by the Serbian military forces, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness has answered. He said that he didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness said that he didn't know about it, Mr. Mikulicic, but I think he was at that moment responding to a question about that very moment, and now Mr. Mikulicic bit as a surprise refreshes his memory with the whole war period, which of course might not be the same. But do you have any further knowledge about specifically Serbs rather than Croats during the war, shelling Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. It was not my focus. We were moving into Knin, and that was the focus of that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But for the remainder of other periods during the war, are you aware of who would be the primary party to shell Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today I'm not. Probably at that time I had a fresher memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we follow the route that you marked in red on this map, and if we go back to your testimony, we're going to pass through the towns of Otocac and Gospic. My question is similar to the one that I asked in reference to Karlovac. I'm referring to paragraph 18 of your statement, where you say that you came to Otocac and that you saw military traces of damage to houses from shelling. My question is, Were you aware at the time or today who had shelled Otocac or, rather, which party to the conflict throughout the whole war held Otocac in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I understand, sir, at that time -- I understood at that time that there had been an exchange of fire, and which damage was caused by who, I don't know, and I was reporting on war damage at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. After that, you came to Gospic, and you said you saw the churches were shelled and that that was the first time that you noticed - and I'm referring back to paragraph 20 of your statement - that that was the first time you noticed smoke. Are you aware, again, who it was who shelled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question started: "And you said you saw the churches were shelled." When I read paragraph 20, I see that: "I saw that a church had been shelled." Therefore, you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I will find -- I will follow your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question, sir, is this: Are you aware who shelled Gospic during the conflict? Which side also held Gospic in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: You were referring, sir, to that -- to paragraph 20 or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. To paragraph 20 and paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes. About paragraph 20, that's -- I refer to my -- to my notes. That had been written on that very afternoon. That's between Licki Osik and Gospic. Indeed, a church was bombarded. There was fire and smoke on the countryside, and I did see, I did observe a group of tanks, tanks, I mean not -- not armed vehicles but tanks with a cupola and a gun, and the barrel, the barrel of that gun was still smoking, so I concluded that that tank, and it was a Croatian tank, had just fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you notice in which direction? Did you notice that, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: It's an interpretation. My interpretation was that that tank -- and I was very surprised by that. I had not expected that that Croatian tank had shelled farms and had put fire on that farm. But, again, that's an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't had time to go through all of the disclosures in this case, but if the witness has -- I believe has indicated, in answer to Mr. Mikulicic' question -- let me find the exact line. Line 17 of page 35, he says that I refer to -- to my notes. I don't believe we have ever been disclosed a copy of any notes, contemporaneous notes that the witness has taken, and to the extent that he has them in court, we would ask that -- to see if we can get a copy of the witness's notes, if they are contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We -- Ms. Mahindaratne, the witness earlier said that he had his notes with him. Are there specific reasons why you have not -- do you have a copy of the notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The witness brought his notes to proofing sessions, and he said that he has his notes, and during the proofing session, of course, he went through it. We did not obtain a copy, nor did I examine his notes. They were his personal notes, and I told him he was free to bring it to court, and if the Defence wishes to examine the notes, the Defence -- I would have no objection, Mr. President. But we did not think it was necessary to obtain his personal notes, which he has kept in his custody all along, and the witness did not turn it over to the members of the Office of the Prosecutor at the time he made the statement to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We never asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am aware of a precedent in the Krajisnik case where I believe a similar situation arose where a witness brought contemporaneous notes into Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that a journalist as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because there, of course -- let's first ask the witness what his position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to share your notes with the parties, which would mean that most likely the Chamber might see them sooner or later as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no objection, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no objections. Are they in such a form that it can be easily copied? I can imagine that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. They can easily be copied. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And these notes you have brought with you, do they cover -- what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe for your Court, the most interesting would be about that Tuesday, 8th of August, I would suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then up to and -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To the extent he has notes from, let's say, 4 August to whenever he left the theatre, that would -- that is what we would consider to be relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then another question. In what language are these notes written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were written first in Dutch, but, of course, it's written on that very afternoon, intense conditions, and I have a personal system of taking notes. Sometimes it's only words, are you writing on the right hand page, on the left hand page. It is up to you. I have no problem, but it's maybe rather difficult to find your way in that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that from apart from the language, which I might be the only one who could read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I have someone on staff who speaks both Belgian and Dutch, so we would be able to go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, the Belgian language is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well -- sorry. He's from Belgium, so -- he's from Belgium. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Some Belgians say they speak Flemish, and others say they speak in the Walloonic language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We could call it B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try -- let's see how we can -- how we can have these notes copied because I take it that you would like to keep the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like so, but I -- I leave it to you, sir. Anyway, if he's speaking about that full week, it is covering two books, two books like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Practical solution for this. As a matter of fact, I would like to invite you to give the originals at this very moment to Mr. Usher, which would disable you to further consult your notes during the examination, which I don't know to what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether that would be a problem for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a problem, but I think it is helpful if I can go through my original notes of that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now, of course I am a bit stuck here at this moment because the parties would like to see it as soon as they can. Is there any way that you could just briefly, if the parties would agree, just briefly give the two notes to Mr. Usher so that we can see how much material it is and to see how quickly it could be copied. Yes. If you would just give it to Mr. Usher so that I can have a look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe one of the reasons I did not think it was necessary for the Prosecution to ask for these notes during the course of the proofing is because it seemed to me as if what is stated, what is noted in the notebooks are practically reproduced in the witness's statements, and that's how I understood because he practically repeated what was given in the statements, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that the Defence wants to verify that. That's what -- Let me just -- I'm looking at it. You'd said the period covers two of these books.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm taking quite extensive notes, but they are also very precise. And that was by purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this, for example, I see here a date of September 16th. Is that already in this book or -- I'm just trying to identify ... I'm not reading it all. I'm just trying to find where it -- where to find dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That book starts with the trip from Zagreb over Karlovac to -- to Knin and Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if you allow, sir, my statement, my written statement or my -- my testimony is almost literally following those notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to ... I'm just trying to find a clue to as how much copying would be needed because your statement goes until ... Yes, your statement is mainly about Karlovac and how you travelled, and that's the -- is there any way that you could indicate in this booklet where approximately your statement stops? Because the first day is quite clear, that is to say Karlovac where the -- where the red tag is. Is there any way that the witness would be provided with a similar tag to see where -- yes, I see. Mr. -- well, from all sides we get text. Would it be possible for you to indicate where, approximately where your statement stops, where it stops in this booklet? And then I suggest - Mr. Misetic, you asked for it - that we ask that portion to be copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, that portion up to where it ends but also if -- he does make references to a few days prior to his trip, so to the extent that the 4th of August onward can be copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is Wednesday -- so the Tuesday, Tuesday is this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But for example, paragraph 6, Your Honour, talks about his arrival in Zagreb on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you try to organise this, Mr. Vanderostyne. Could you put a tag not on the day where you left -- where you were in Karlovac and where you left, but two or three days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prior to that, yes. Or are we, then, in the other booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the other booklet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the other booklet. Mr. Misetic, we're now in the other booklet. Let's, then, first focus on -- Could you perhaps in the other booklet indicate three, four days before the new booklet starts? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just refresh the witness's recollection. He speaks in paragraph 6 of a meeting with Brigadier Peeters. If I could have the notes of that, and it actually references that you arrived on the 5th of August, so from the 5th of August onward, I would be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could just -- it doesn't make much sense to explain everything to Mr. Usher who is not in a position to -- If you could find where it starts on -- I think you said on the 5th of August, Mr. Misetic, to put a marker there. And then in the next book, starting with Karlovac, that you take -- let me just -- I think that the last event described there is about what happened in Cenici at some ten kilometres south of Knin on the way to Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That -- could you please put a tag there as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. It is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, could I then have both booklets. Yes, is there -- Mr. Registrar, is there any way that we could have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, we'll try to do a quick copying exercise. Mr. Misetic, from what I've seen already, and it might be quite a job to have this put in a format which is legible. I think most of it would be very difficult to read, as a matter of fact, although you could decipher some words. But let's first -- then at least it is available, and then the parties can further consider what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could -- when the first full book is copied, could the other book perhaps remain in the hands of the witness because that seems to be the -- or that that is first copied, the second book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that there were also some loose leafs in there, in the books. That apparently is not part of the sequence of notes. First, the beginning of the second booklet will be copied so that that can be returned immediately to you so that it's available for further consultation. Mr. Mikulicic, after this intermezzo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not receive English translation on channel 4 at this moment. Could you please re-start, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you speak English, Mr. Mikulicic, then it's a bit difficult to verify whether the translation is okay, but I appreciate your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I try to communicate directly from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vanderostyne, the topic that we touched upon before the intermezzo, as His Honour the Presiding Judge said, you were not aware that the cities of Karlovac, Gospic, and Otocac were in Croatian hands and that they were shelled and bombarded by the Serbian side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: My conclusion is there had been war and both sides had -- had been in confrontation and both sides had been used to arms. That was my -- that was my conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, that's a very logical reply but not to my question, Mr. Vanderostyne. I asked you, were you aware that the towns of Karlovac, Gospic, and Otocac were in Croatian hands and that they were bombarded by Serbian military forces? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: You're referring to when? When were they in Croatian hands?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: So Karlovac, yes, sure, sure. Otocac, yes, sure. Gospic, I could not -- no, I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Your route further continued in the direction of Gracac, and you went through numerous villages that you said had been burned and destroyed and so on and so forth. This was a territory of the former Republic of the Serbian Krajina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that this territory that was the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that earlier on in some of those villages Croatians lived as well?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: Sure I did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your journey when you noticed these damages to the buildings, were you able to tell apart, to differentiate between the buildings that had been destroyed earlier and those that were destroyed during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: In general, I was able. Yes, sir. You could see the ruins of what I call the -- what is it, the 1991 war or -- when the Serbia or Serb troops had conquered Croatian territory. You could see those ruins. Those were old ruins. They had been overgrown, and they were not burning. Those were clearly old ruins that you could very -- very well make the difference between old ruins and fresh -- fresh burning. Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, would you please now see a short video-clip together with us. It is about three minutes long. This is 3D00-0814. Just to say that this is a video-clip that was recorded on the 5th of August, 1995, when the logistics forces of the Special Police entered Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, did you go through this village, Sveti Rok? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: I don't know this video, sir. I can only -- I can only give testimony about what I have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, and it is very good that you make this observation. The question was, I don't know whether you on your way you passed through any village by the name of Sveti Rok.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remind that -- I do not recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Sempre Gracac, here we go. This could be Ricice here; also was a Croatian village. You know it's a Croatian village as it was burnt down. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, do you remember that on your way to Gracac you went through the village of Ricice?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not. I do not recall that name, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the route that you marked on the map, both of these villages are on the route, both Sveti Rok and Ricice. That is the reason why I was asking whether you could recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Everything is really burnt down here. Where is the eff UNPROFOR now to ask whose [illegible]."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Here, Mr. Vanderostyne, you see this sign-post to Gracac. It is not very legible, but can you read it, actually. Can you recall this?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, I do not recall it, but I imagine I have seen it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Gracac. On a bicycle, huh?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, you could see that this is the entry to Gracac. Can you recall the UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you said -- could we turn back. You said this is the entrance of Gracac. Where do we see that, and where is the witness supposed to see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's -- yes, yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the witness -- yes. The witness gives evidence, Mr. Mikulicic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] It's the UNPROFOR base, okay. There are still a few of those antennas."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, do you remember this intersection at the very approach, on the very approaches to Gracac, where you go -- if you turn to the right, you would go to the railway station; to the left, you would go to Gracac; and if you continue straight on, that would be the road to Zagreb and further on to the north?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: No, sir. Excuse me, but this is 13 years ago. I only rely on my own notes, what I -- and I stick to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is no reason to apologise. Just tell us if you don't know, and if you would know, please tell us as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's been a long time, and of course you cannot recall every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Buffet Joco."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We're now in Gracac downtown. This is a buffet called Joco. Can you recall this location?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderostyne, now we're in Gracac. You said that you went through Gracac. You cannot, of course, confirm this, but I'm telling you that this is the route that you took and that you then went back and stopped at the main square.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND VANDEROSTYNE
utterances.text: That's right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, may I first ask you, is this the route the witness took, and is it the route as he took it? That means that he came from Karlovac and then turning to the south and then more to the east or is it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is precisely the route that the witness took on that very day, between villages Sveti Rok and the exit of Gracac, so this is precisely that route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the things that came into my mind, that there was a clear sign that you would head for a -- not an intersection but how you call it, a three -- where to the right it went to Zagreb and to the left it went to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was on the exit of the village of Gracac, where the cross-roads is. You can remember that we were talking about this cross-roads that has been shelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just -- Mr. Mikulicic in fact suggested to the witness that this was the route that the witness took, but we have no indication as to who made this tape. Now, there's a indication it's 5th -- on 5th August 1995. I don't know whether Mr. Mikulicic intends to call the witness or someone who was present while this footage was made to clearly indicate what areas this camera is being taken through. Considering that the witness does not recognise the scenery, I do not see a basis for Mr. Mikulicic to suggest that this was in fact the route that the witness took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, could you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What I could propose, Your Honour -- yes. It is my statement that this was the route based on the witness facts which he took on that particular day. I was hoping that the witness would recognise the route that he took, but, unfortunately he did not. There is no other way towards Gracac from the direction of Sveti Rok and Ricice. There is only a south road around Gracac that the witness obviously did not take that day.
